title: What are the requirements to enter heaven?
dek: Scripture states one condition rather than a list: faith in Jesus Christ, received as a gift rather than earned as a standard. What that means for good works, repentance, baptism — and whether a person can know.
imageAlt: An open wooden door in a dark wall, looking out onto a sunrise over a valley and a lake, with a paved path running from the doorway towards the light and rays falling across the threshold.
body:
Entry into heaven rests on faith in Jesus Christ, not on personal goodness or religious effort. Jesus said no one comes to the Father except through Him. Repentance turns a person toward God, and a changed life follows — but that change is the fruit of salvation, not the price paid for it.

## What does the Bible say is required?

Faith in Jesus Christ. Scripture states it as a single condition rather than a list, and Jesus said it about Himself in the plainest terms:

> I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
> — John 14:6, KJV

Peter said the same before the council in Jerusalem, telling them there is no other name given among men by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12).

Paul then explains why it works this way — and the reason matters as much as the requirement:

> For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.
> — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV

A gift is received, not earned. That single distinction shapes everything else on this page.

## Is being a good person enough to enter heaven?

No. Scripture presents salvation as a gift received rather than a standard achieved.

The difficulty with a goodness standard is that nobody knows where the line sits — and Scripture never sets one. It says instead that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God (Romans 3:23), which puts everyone on the same side of the line.

Isaiah goes further, describing even human righteousness as filthy rags (Isaiah 64:6). That is not a comment on human worth. It is a comment on what human effort can purchase from God.

There is a mercy hidden in this. If entry depended on goodness, no one could ever know whether they had done enough.

## Where do Christians disagree about faith and works?

Christians agree that salvation comes through Christ. They differ on how faith and works relate to one another, and it is worth stating both sides honestly.

James writes that faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Paul writes that salvation is not of works, so that no one can boast (Ephesians 2:9). Both statements are in the same Bible, and Christians have read the relationship between them differently for five hundred years.

::note Where this article stands
:: Some traditions read James and Paul as describing one reality from two angles — Paul explaining how salvation is received, James explaining how genuine faith shows itself. Others draw the line differently. This article follows the position that works are the evidence of saving faith rather than its cause: a living faith produces a changed life, but the change is not the payment.

Read that way, the question “have I done enough good works?” is the wrong question. The right one is whether a person has come to Christ at all.

## What part does repentance play?

Repentance is the turning that faith involves. It is not a separate requirement stacked on top of believing — the New Testament consistently treats the two as one movement.

When the crowd at Pentecost asked what they should do, Peter's answer began with repentance (Acts 2:38). Paul described his own preaching as testifying to repentance toward God and faith toward the Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 20:21). Jesus was blunter still, saying that unless people repent they will perish (Luke 13:3).

Repentance means turning away from sin and turning back to God. A person cannot come to Christ while holding on to what they are asking to be forgiven for. More on [why repentance matters](/articles/what-is-the-importance-of-repentance).

## Do I have to be baptised or join a church?

Baptism and belonging to a church are both commanded in Scripture, and neither is presented as the thing that saves.

The clearest evidence is the man crucified beside Jesus. He was never baptised, joined no congregation, performed no good works, and had hours to live. He simply asked to be remembered. The answer came immediately:

> Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
> — Luke 23:43, KJV

That account rules out any requirement a dying man could not have met. Baptism follows faith as obedience, and church is where a believer grows — but the thief entered paradise without either.

## Can a person know they are going to heaven?

Scripture says yes, and treats assurance as something believers are meant to have rather than hope for.

> These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life.
> — 1 John 5:13, KJV

The word is *know*. But notice where the certainty rests. It does not depend on how strong a person feels, or on a good week. It rests on what Christ has done, which does not change with the state of anyone's feelings.

Jesus put it as a promise with no exception attached: whoever comes to Him will not be cast out (John 6:37).

## The short answer

One requirement, not many: come to Christ. Turn from what you are asking to be forgiven for, and receive what cannot be bought.

Everything else — baptism, holy living, service, church — belongs to the life that follows. It is fruit, not fee.
